events.title: Safari 3 for Windows released
events.summary: Apple released Safari 3 for Windows on June 11, 2007 at WWDC — bringing WebKit to PC users for the first time.
events.about: Safari on Windows let web developers test WebKit rendering without a Mac and briefly gave Windows users an Apple browser option. It spread WebKit's engine beyond macOS — a precursor to Chrome adopting WebKit and later forking Blink.

narrative.whyChosen: Safari for Windows exported Apple's engine to the PC ecosystem.
narrative.whyImportant: WebKit on Windows influenced cross-browser testing and engine adoption before Chrome.
narrative.problemSolved: Developers on Windows could not easily test Safari/WebKit behavior for their sites.

events.title: Heroku founded
events.summary: Adam Wiggins, James Lindenbaum, and Orion Henry founded Heroku in June 2007 — a platform-as-a-service for deploying Ruby apps with git push.
events.about: Heroku abstracted servers behind `git push heroku master`: dynos, buildpacks, and add-ons for Postgres, Redis, and logging. Developers stopped provisioning VMs and focused on code. The model influenced Cloud Foundry, Render, Fly.io, and how teams think about twelve-factor apps — even after Salesforce acquired Heroku in 2010.

narrative.whyChosen: Heroku pioneered developer-friendly PaaS with git-based deploys and managed runtimes.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved many teams would trade server control for faster shipping on a managed platform.
narrative.problemSolved: Small teams could not afford dedicated ops staff but still needed reliable production hosting.

events.title: iPhone goes on sale
events.summary: Apple began selling the iPhone in the United States on June 29, 2007 — six months after its Macworld introduction.
events.about: The iPhone put a capacitive touchscreen, mobile Safari, and eventually the App Store in millions of pockets. Developers pivoted to mobile-first web design, native iOS SDKs, and responsive CSS. Mobile traffic overtook desktop on many sites — all tracing to this product reaching consumers.

narrative.whyChosen: The iPhone's retail launch turned a keynote demo into the defining smartphone platform for developers.
narrative.whyImportant: It made mobile web and native app development mandatory skills for mainstream software teams.
narrative.problemSolved: Phones offered poor mobile browsing; users needed a pocket computer with a real web browser and touch UI.
